lessons.title: Reading a quote
lessons.summary: Last price, change, percent change, volume and range: the five numbers you see everywhere.

steps.title: Find a symbol
steps.body: Your watchlist sits in the left rail. Each row is one symbol with its latest price and today's move. Click a row to make it the selected symbol; linked widgets follow it.
steps.try: Click any symbol in the list.

steps.title: Last price and change
steps.body: The big number is the last traded price. Change and percent change are measured from the previous regular-session close, not from when you opened the app. Green means above yesterday's close, red below.
steps.try: Compare two symbols by percent change rather than by price.

steps.title: Volume and range
steps.body: Volume counts shares traded today; compare it with average volume to see whether today is busy. The day range shows today's low and high, and where the last price sits inside it.
steps.try: Look for a symbol whose last price is near the top of its day range.

steps.title: Bid, ask and spread
steps.body: If your data plan includes them, bid is what buyers offer and ask is what sellers want. The gap between them, the spread, is a cost you would pay to trade. Wide spreads usually mean thin trading.
steps.try: Open the quote widget for a symbol and check whether bid/ask are available from your provider.

lessons.title: Data, delays and providers
lessons.summary: Where prices come from, why they can be late, and how this app tells you.

steps.title: Demo or live
steps.body: This chip shows where data is coming from. DEMO means simulated prices for learning: they are not real. Add a free API key in Settings to switch to a live provider.
steps.try: Hover the chip to see the current source.

steps.title: Delayed is normal
steps.body: Many free plans deliver prices 15 minutes late, or only from one exchange venue. Every quote has a timestamp; when it stops advancing during an open session, the app marks it stale instead of pretending it is live.
steps.try: Look for a quote time on a card or the quote widget.

steps.title: Market sessions
steps.body: The session chip works out from your device clock whether the market is pre-market, open, after-hours or closed, using a local holiday calendar. A dashed border means the calendar cannot vouch for that date.
steps.try: Click the session chip to see the next open or close.

steps.title: API limits
steps.body: Free keys allow a limited number of requests per minute or day. The quota meter shows how much you have used. Watching fewer symbols, or refreshing less often, makes the quota last.
steps.try: Change the refresh interval and watch the meter.

lessons.title: Candlesticks in two minutes
lessons.summary: How one candle summarises open, high, low and close, and why the timeframe matters.

steps.title: Body and wicks
steps.body: A candle's body runs from the open to the close. Its thin wicks reach the high and the low. A green (up) candle closed above where it opened; a red (down) candle closed below.
steps.try: Hover a candle to read its open, high, low and close.

steps.title: One candle, one period
steps.body: Each candle covers one interval: a minute, an hour, a day. The same stock can look calm on a daily chart and wild on a 1-minute chart. Pick the range first (1D, 1M, 1Y), then the interval.
steps.try: Switch between 1D and 1Y and notice how the candle size changes.

steps.title: Gaps
steps.body: When a candle opens far from the previous close, a gap appears. Gaps usually come from news released while the market was closed.
steps.try: Find a gap on a daily chart.

steps.title: Simpler views
steps.body: A line chart joins the closes and hides the wicks, which is less noisy when you are starting out. Heikin-Ashi candles are smoothed averages: good for seeing trends, but they are not real prices.
steps.try: Switch the chart type to Line, then back to Candles.

lessons.title: How alerts work here
lessons.summary: Rules that watch for you. They notify; they never trade.

steps.title: Open the rules
steps.body: Alerts are rules that run in your browser each time prices refresh. They only notify you; nothing is ever bought or sold.
steps.try: Open the alerts panel.

steps.title: Above versus crosses above
steps.body: 'Above' is a state: it is true for as long as the price stays above the level. 'Crosses above' is an event: it fires only at the moment of crossing. For most price levels, crossing is what you want.
steps.try: Create a 'crosses above' rule a little above the current price of a symbol.

steps.title: Once or re-arm
steps.body: 'Once' fires one time and stops. 'Re-arm' fires again after the condition resets. Confirmation makes the rule wait for several refreshes in a row, which filters brief spikes.
steps.try: Set a rule to 'once' and add 2 ticks of confirmation.

steps.title: Beyond price
steps.body: Rules can watch percent change, gaps, volume spikes, 52-week highs, moving-average crosses, RSI levels, trailing stops and your whole portfolio. Each type has a '?' explaining what it measures.
steps.try: Browse the rule types and open the help for one you do not know.

steps.title: Know the limits
steps.body: Rules run only while this page is open, and they are only as fresh as your data. On a delayed feed, an alert fires late.
steps.try: Turn on browser notifications in Settings if you want alerts while the tab is in the background.

lessons.title: Trends and moving averages
lessons.summary: Seeing direction through the noise, and why every average lags.

steps.title: Higher highs, higher lows
steps.body: An uptrend is a series of higher highs and higher lows; a downtrend is the reverse. Trends exist on every timeframe and can disagree with each other.
steps.try: On a 1Y daily chart, decide whether the stock is trending up, down or sideways.

steps.title: Add a moving average
steps.body: A moving average smooths the price. The 50-day and 200-day simple averages are the most widely followed. Price above a rising 200-day is often described as a long-term uptrend.
steps.try: Add SMA 50 and SMA 200 to the chart.

steps.title: Crosses
steps.body: When the 50-day crosses above the 200-day it is called a golden cross; below, a death cross. Both are late by design: averages describe the past.
steps.try: Find the last time the two averages crossed.

steps.title: Turn it into an alert
steps.body: Instead of checking charts every day, a rule can notify you when price crosses a moving average, or when two averages cross.
steps.try: Create a 'price crosses SMA(200)' alert for one symbol.

lessons.title: Volume: the effort behind a move
lessons.summary: Why the same move means more on heavy volume, and how to spot unusual activity.

steps.title: Volume bars
steps.body: The bars under the price show how many shares traded in each period. Green bars belong to up candles, red to down candles.
steps.try: Turn the volume pane on and find the tallest bar of the last month.

steps.title: Normal versus unusual
steps.body: A volume average line shows what is normal. Relative volume (RVOL) divides today's volume by the average: 3x means three times the usual activity.
steps.try: Compare today's volume with the average volume in the quote widget.

steps.title: Early in the day
steps.body: Daily volume starts at zero each morning, so a full-day comparison makes mornings look quiet. Keep that in mind before reading too much into low numbers.
steps.try: Create a relative-volume alert at 2x for a symbol you follow.

lessons.title: RSI and momentum
lessons.summary: Measuring the speed of moves, and why 'overbought' is not a sell signal.

steps.title: What RSI measures
steps.body: RSI compares the size of recent up moves with recent down moves on a 0 to 100 scale. It measures speed, not value.
steps.try: Add RSI (14) as a pane under the chart.

steps.title: 70 and 30
steps.body: Readings above 70 are called overbought and below 30 oversold. In strong trends RSI can stay above 70 for weeks, so these labels describe, they do not predict.
steps.try: Find a period where RSI stayed above 70 while the price kept rising.

steps.title: MACD
steps.body: MACD is the gap between two exponential averages, with a signal line. Crosses of MACD and its signal are read as momentum shifts; they lag, like all averages.
steps.try: Add MACD and compare its crosses with the price chart.

steps.title: Divergence
steps.body: When price makes a new high but RSI makes a lower high, momentum is not confirming the move. Divergences can last a long time, so treat them as context.
steps.try: Look for one divergence on a 1Y chart.

lessons.title: Support and resistance
lessons.summary: Levels where price has paused before, and how to mark them.

steps.title: Zones, not lines
steps.body: Support is where falling prices have tended to stop; resistance where rising prices have stalled. Previous highs and lows, round numbers and the 52-week high are common examples.
steps.try: Find a price where the stock turned around at least twice.

steps.title: Mark the level
steps.body: Use the horizontal-line tool to mark a level. Drawings are saved per symbol on this device.
steps.try: Draw a horizontal line at a level you found.

steps.title: Breakouts
steps.body: A close through resistance on heavy volume is called a breakout. Many breakouts fail and fall back, so some people wait for a close beyond the level.
steps.try: Right-click (or long-press) the line and choose 'Alert at this price'.

lessons.title: Risk and position sizing
lessons.summary: Decide what you can lose before deciding what you hope to gain. Educational, not advice.

steps.title: Start with the loss
steps.body: A common educational rule is to risk only a small, fixed share of an account on any one idea, such as 1%. On a 50,000 account that is 500.
steps.try: Write down the maximum you would accept losing on one position.

steps.title: Stop distance sets the size
steps.body: Shares = money at risk / (entry - stop). With entry 40 and stop 37, risk is 3 per share, so 500 of risk allows about 166 shares.
steps.try: Use the position-size calculator with your own numbers.

steps.title: Reward versus risk
steps.body: If the target is 46, the reward is 6 against a risk of 3: a 2:1 ratio. At 2:1 you would break even being right one time in three, before costs.
steps.try: Compute the break-even win rate for a 1.5:1 setup.

steps.title: What a stop cannot do
steps.body: Stops do not protect against gaps: a stock can open far below your level. Leverage makes this worse, because losses can exceed what you put in.
steps.try: Set a trailing-stop alert on a position to watch your exit without placing an order.

lessons.title: Diversification and allocation
lessons.summary: Spreading risk so that one bad outcome does not sink everything.

steps.title: Many eggs, many baskets
steps.body: A single company can lose half its value on bad news. A fund holding hundreds of companies rarely does because of one of them. Diversifying reduces company-specific risk, not market risk.
steps.try: Open your holdings and count how many separate companies you really own.

steps.title: Look at the mix
steps.body: Allocation shows your money by asset class, sector, country, currency or account. Several ETFs can hold the same giant companies, so check the overlap.
steps.try: Group your portfolio by sector and by currency.

steps.title: Targets and drift
steps.body: If you set target weights, drift shows how far each holding has moved from its target as prices change. The app only shows drift; what to do about it is your decision.
steps.try: Set a target weight for one holding and watch its drift.

lessons.title: Fees and taxes basics
lessons.summary: The costs you can control, and why the ledger matters at tax time. Informational only.

steps.title: Costs are certain
steps.body: Commissions, spreads, fund expense ratios and currency conversion all reduce returns, and unlike returns they are guaranteed. Frequent small trades add up quickly.
steps.try: Estimate what you paid in fees last year.

steps.title: Record every transaction
steps.body: Buys, sells, dividends, fees and splits each go in the ledger. With dates and fees recorded, the app can work out cost basis, realized gains and income.
steps.try: Add a past purchase with its real date and fee.

steps.title: Lot methods
steps.body: FIFO sells the oldest shares first; average cost uses one blended price. They give different realized gains for the same trades. Your country's tax rules decide which applies.
steps.try: Switch the cost method in Settings and compare realized P/L.

steps.title: Not tax advice
steps.body: Figures here are informational. Your broker's official statements and a qualified professional are the authorities on what you owe.
steps.try: Export the realized-gains CSV to keep with your records.

lessons.title: Pro tips
lessons.summary: Keyboard control, linked multi-chart layouts, screens and indicator alerts.

steps.title: Keyboard on charts
steps.body: Click a chart to focus it, then use + and - to zoom, the arrow keys to pan, Home and End to jump, and double-click to reset the view.
steps.try: Zoom into last week using only the keyboard.

steps.title: Multi-chart layouts
steps.body: Add several chart widgets to one tab. Linked widgets follow the selected symbol; unlink one to pin it, for example to keep SPY next to the stock you are studying. Crosshairs can be synced across charts.
steps.try: Add a second chart, pin it to an index and compare.

steps.title: Compare and relative strength
steps.body: Overlay another symbol on a chart in percent terms, or divide one by the other, to see which has led over the period.
steps.try: Compare a stock with its sector ETF over 1Y.

steps.title: Screens
steps.body: Screens filter your symbols by conditions such as distance from the 52-week high, RSI or relative volume. Presets are starting points for research, not recommendations.
steps.try: Run a preset screen and save a modified copy.

steps.title: Indicator alerts
steps.body: Rules can fire on MACD signal crosses, Bollinger Band breaks, moves larger than k x ATR and moving-average crosses. They use daily bars, so they cost extra API calls; keep the list focused.
steps.try: Create an ATR-move alert with k = 2 on a volatile symbol.
